notes.meaning: When Peter arrived at the house, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet to show him great honor. Cornelius may have viewed Peter as a divine messenger or an angel worthy of the highest reverence. Falling down like this was a customary way of showing deep respect in the ancient Near East, but it went beyond what was proper for any human being.

Peter immediately pulled Cornelius back up to his feet and refused this kind of bow. He reminded the Roman officer that he was merely a human being like him, not God or an angel. Peter knew that true worship belongs solely to God.

Peter kept conversing with Cornelius as they stepped inside the house. There he discovered a large crowd of family and friends waiting eagerly to hear what he had to say. Walking into a Gentile's home was a bold step, showing that Peter was already setting aside old barriers.

Peter explained to the room that Jewish tradition strictly forbade Jews from visiting or eating with foreigners to avoid becoming ritually unclean. However, the vision of the sheet with animals had taught Peter a deeper truth. God had shown him that no group of people should be treated as impure or excluded from His love.

Because God had changed his understanding, Peter traveled to Caesarea without making any excuses or arguing back. Even though he had heard a brief report from Cornelius's messengers, Peter asked Cornelius to explain directly why he had called for him. This allowed Cornelius to tell his own story before everyone present.

Cornelius explained that four days earlier, around three in the afternoon, he had been praying in his home. During his prayer, an angel appearing like a man in dazzling, bright clothing suddenly stood in front of him. This took place at the traditional Jewish hour of evening prayer.

The angel told Cornelius that God had noticed his sincere prayers and his generosity to the needy. The angel then gave exact directions to send messengers to the seaside town of Joppa to summon Simon Peter. God did not have the angel preach the gospel himself, but arranged for a human messenger to bring the good news.

Cornelius explained that he obeyed God at once by sending for Peter, and he warmly thanked Peter for being gracious enough to come. The whole household was gathered together with open hearts, recognizing that God was watching them. They were completely ready to hear whatever message the Lord had given Peter to share.

Peter solemnly began his message with the realization that had just become clear to him. He saw without a doubt that God does not favor people based on their nationality, race, or outward background. God judges fairly and does not give special privileges simply because someone was born a Jew.

God accepts anyone from any nation who reveres Him and strives to live righteously. Peter did not mean people earn salvation by good deeds, but that nationality is no barrier to God's mercy. Those who truly seek God are drawn by His grace to hear and receive the message of Christ.

differ.view: John Piper emphasizes that Cornelius was not yet saved before hearing Peter preach, but that God was pleased with his genuine search and brought him the gospel so he could be saved through faith.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic writers cite the case of Cornelius to show that God can give grace and salvation to non-Christians who seek him sincerely, outside the normal sacrament of baptism.

notes.meaning: God first announced this good news of peace to the people of Israel, offering reconciliation between God and humanity through Jesus Christ. Peter emphasized that Jesus is not just the Messiah of the Jews, but the sovereign Lord over every people and nation. That universal rule is the reason peace is now offered to everyone everywhere.

Peter noted that his listeners had already heard reports about the events that had stirred the region. The public ministry of Jesus had become widely known across the land of Judea after John the Baptist began preaching and baptizing. Peter started with the facts they already knew to lead them into the full truth about Jesus.

God publicly set Jesus apart and empowered Him at His baptism by giving Him the Holy Spirit without measure. With that divine authority, Jesus traveled through towns healing the sick and freeing those held in demonic bondage. His works of mercy proved beyond question that God was truly with Him.

Peter and the other apostles were direct eyewitnesses of everything Jesus said and did in Galilee, Judea, and the capital city of Jerusalem. Yet despite His good deeds, the authorities rejected Jesus and executed Him by nailing Him to a wooden cross. Referring to the cross as a tree echoed the Old Testament idea of a shameful execution.

Death could not hold Jesus, and God raised Him back to life on the third day. The risen Lord did not show Himself to the whole general public, but appeared to chosen witnesses who knew Him well. The apostles even shared meals with Him after His resurrection, giving certain proof that He was truly alive in bodily form and not a ghost.

The risen Jesus ordered the apostles to proclaim publicly that God has made Him the supreme Judge of all humanity. That judgment covers every person, both those still alive when He returns and those who have already died. Knowing Jesus is the coming Judge shows everyone how vital it is to submit to Him now.

Peter pointed to the entire Old Testament, explaining that the ancient prophets pointed forward to Christ and His kingdom. The heart of their message was that anyone who puts their trust in Jesus receives full forgiveness for their sins. This pardon comes freely as a gift through the authority and sacrifice of His name, with no racial requirement attached.

Before Peter could even finish his sermon, the Holy Spirit came down with power upon everyone listening in the room. God did not wait for the apostles to lay hands on them or for them to be baptized in water first. By pouring out His Spirit directly, God visibly confirmed that He had welcomed these Gentile believers into His family through faith.

The six Jewish believers who had traveled with Peter from Joppa were completely stunned by what took place. They had grown up believing that God's special presence and gifts belonged solely to the Jewish people within their covenant. Seeing the Spirit poured out upon uncircumcised Gentiles shattered their former expectations and proved God had opened the door to the nations.

The Jewish companions knew the Holy Spirit had arrived because they heard the Gentile believers speaking in miraculous, unlearned languages and praising God. Just as on the day of Pentecost, the Spirit prompted a public outpouring of praise to honor the Lord. This clear supernatural sign left no doubt that God had accepted them completely.

differ.view: In official Assemblies of God teaching, speaking in tongues is the "initial physical evidence"—the first outward, visible sign—that a believer has received the baptism in the Holy Spirit (a special empowering by God). They teach that Peter and his companions only knew these Gentiles had received the Spirit because they heard them speak in tongues.

Teachers on Bible.org explain that speaking in tongues here was a unique historical sign given to convince Peter and the Jewish Christians that God was now welcoming Gentiles on equal terms. They teach that this event marked the gospel crossing a major cultural barrier, rather than establishing tongues as a required sign for every Christian who receives the Spirit today.

Teachers from this viewpoint (who believe supernatural gifts are still active today, but that not all believers speak in tongues) explain that tongues here were simply one way the Spirit released joyful worship to magnify God. They teach that speaking in tongues may or may not happen, while the essential evidence of the Holy Spirit's presence is a heart that honors God instead of self.

notes.meaning: Peter challenged anyone present to find a reason why these new Gentile converts should not receive water baptism. Since God had already given them the inward reality of the Holy Spirit, it made no sense to deny them the outward sign of belonging to the church. They stood on exactly the same ground of grace as the Jewish disciples.

differ.view: Water baptism is an outward sign and seal of grace already bestowed by the Spirit, showing that baptism does not produce regeneration.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: God is not bound by the sacraments, but water baptism remains necessary by Christ's command and is properly given even when the Spirit is received beforehand.

notes.meaning: Peter directed that the new believers be baptized by water in the authority and name of Jesus Christ, likely having his Jewish companions perform the baptisms. After being baptized, Cornelius and his household urged Peter to remain with them for several days. This allowed Peter to provide deeper teaching in the faith and cemented fellowship between Jewish and Gentile Christians.
